question: What companies can I hire a Chief Revenue Officer from?
body:
## Direct Answer

You can hire a Chief Revenue Officer from three broad talent pools: retained executive search firms (Heidrick & Struggles, Spencer Stuart, Korn Ferry, Russell Reynolds Associates, Egon Zehnder), specialist go-to-market and revenue-focused recruiters (True Search, Betts Recruiting, Sales Talent Agency, CloserIQ), and direct-sourcing channels like your own network, portfolio-company CROs, and vetted fractional-CRO marketplaces. The "right company to hire from" is less about a single vendor and more about matching the search channel to your stage, budget, and the specific revenue problem you need solved.

Most founders and CEOs treat "where do I find a CRO?" as a vendor-selection question when it's really a sequencing question. A Series A startup poaching a rising VP of Sales from a scaled competitor runs a completely different play than a private-equity-backed company that needs a proven operator to double revenue before an exit. This essay maps the four real channels — retained search, contingency/specialist recruiters, fractional marketplaces, and direct sourcing — explains what each one actually costs you in fees and time, and gives you a decision framework so you stop paying enterprise search prices for a startup-stage hire (or vice versa). By the end you should be able to name the single channel that fits your situation, know roughly what it will cost in both dollars and founder hours, and understand how to evaluate a candidate's source company without being seduced by a famous logo.

## Which executive search firms actually place Chief Revenue Officers?

The top of the market is the retained search world, and a handful of firms genuinely own the C-suite mandate. Spencer Stuart, Heidrick & Struggles, Korn Ferry, Russell Reynolds Associates, and Egon Zehnder are the "big five" of retained executive search, and all five run dedicated technology, sales, and go-to-market practices that place CROs at growth-stage and enterprise companies. These firms work on a retainer — you pay in installments regardless of outcome, and the fee is customarily structured as roughly one-third of the executive's first-year total cash compensation. That means for a CRO whose package runs into the mid-six figures plus equity, the search fee is a serious line item, and you're paying for a deeply researched, confidential, off-market process rather than a stack of inbound résumés.

Below the big five sits a strong tier of firms that many high-growth companies actually prefer because they move faster and know the operator layer better. True Search (often branded simply as "True") has become one of the most active placers of go-to-market executives in venture-backed technology, and firms like Daversa Partners specialize almost exclusively in placing leaders — including CROs and VPs of Sales — for startups from Series A through pre-IPO. Riviera Partners, On-Ramps, and boutique GTM shops round out the field. The practical takeaway: if you are a funded startup, a specialist growth-stage firm will usually give you better-fit candidates and a lower effective cost than routing an early-stage mandate through a firm built for Fortune 500 board searches.

There is also a real difference in how these firms *research* a market, and it matters more for a CRO than for almost any other role. A revenue leader is judged on the specific motion they've run — enterprise field sales, product-led growth, channel, or a hybrid — so the value of a good search firm is less its Rolodex and more its ability to build a precise longlist of people who have run *your* motion at *your* next stage. The big five earn their fee on genuinely confidential mandates: a public company replacing an underperforming CRO cannot afford for the market, the sales team, or the current incumbent to learn a search is underway, and a retained firm insulates that process behind researchers who approach candidates without ever naming the client until a mutual-interest bar is cleared. Growth-stage specialists earn their fee a different way — through sheer density in the operator layer, having placed and tracked the same few thousand SaaS revenue leaders across multiple funding cycles, so they can tell you not just who is available but who is genuinely ready to step up a level versus who is coasting on a strong prior market. When you interview firms, ask each one to walk you through two recent CRO searches at your stage and motion; the specificity of that answer, more than the brand on the door, tells you whether they can actually fill your seat.

## What is the difference between retained, contingency, and fractional CRO hiring?

These three models are not interchangeable, and choosing the wrong one is the single most common mistake we see. **Retained search** is an exclusive, paid-in-advance engagement for hard-to-fill senior roles; the firm commits real research hours mapping the market, approaching passive candidates, and managing a confidential process. **Contingency and specialist recruiting** flips the risk — you pay only when a placement is made, which works well for VP-of-Sales and revenue-leader roles that sit just below the true C-suite, or when you have several searches running and want to test channels. **Fractional CRO** engagements skip permanent hiring altogether: you bring in an experienced revenue leader part-time, often through a marketplace or advisory network, to build the go-to-market engine before you're ready to fund a full-time executive.

The decision hinges on stage, urgency, and how defined the role is. A pre-Series-B company that has never had a revenue leader is often better served by a fractional CRO for six to twelve months — you get senior judgment on pricing, comp plans, and pipeline discipline without a full permanent package, and you learn what the role actually needs before you commit. A company with product-market fit and a board mandate to scale needs a permanent hire and should pay for retained or specialist search. The diagram below shows the routing logic.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Need revenue leadership] --> B{Is the role fully defined and funded}
    B -->|No, still building GTM| C[Fractional CRO or advisor]
    B -->|Yes, permanent hire| D{Company stage}
    D -->|Startup to growth| E[Specialist GTM search firm]
    D -->|Enterprise or PE backed| F[Retained big five firm]
    C --> G[Reassess in six to twelve months]
    G --> B
    E --> H[Onboard and set first ninety days]
    F --> H
```

Notice that the fractional path loops back — it's a way to de-risk the eventual permanent search, not a permanent substitute for it. Many companies run a fractional CRO precisely so that when they do launch a retained search, they can write a far sharper scorecard. For the mechanics of scoping the role before you engage anyone, see the deeper breakdown at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/cro-scorecard-design.

One nuance that gets lost in the retained-versus-contingency debate: exclusivity and incentive alignment matter as much as who pays when. A contingency recruiter is paid only on a fill, which sounds founder-friendly until you realize it quietly incentivizes speed and volume over fit — the recruiter's economics reward closing *a* candidate, not necessarily *the* candidate, and they are often working the same search against two or three other firms racing for the same fee. A retained firm, paid regardless of outcome, has no reason to push a marginal candidate across the line and every reason to protect its reputation with your board for the next mandate. That is the real trade you are making: contingency shifts fee-risk to the recruiter but can shift fit-risk onto you, while retained absorbs fit-risk at the cost of a guaranteed, front-loaded fee. Fractional sits outside this axis entirely — you are buying senior *time*, not a permanent placement, so the alignment question becomes whether the fractional leader is genuinely building durable systems that outlast their engagement or simply holding the wheel until you hire. The best fractional CROs actively work to make themselves replaceable, documenting the playbook, comp plan, and hiring bar so the permanent successor inherits a running engine rather than a black box.

## Can I hire a CRO directly from a competitor or my own network?

Yes, and for a large share of successful CRO placements this is exactly what happens — the executive comes through a warm channel, not a firm. The two richest direct-sourcing pools are your investors' networks and your own leadership graph. Venture and private-equity firms maintain talent partners whose entire job is to connect portfolio companies with vetted operators, and a CRO who just scaled a portfolio company through an exit is often the single best introduction your lead investor can make. If you're backed, ask your board for their operating-partner shortlist before you spend a dollar on retained search; the fit is frequently better because the investor already knows both the candidate and your business.

Direct-from-competitor hiring is legitimate and common, but it carries real constraints you must respect. Non-compete enforceability varies dramatically by jurisdiction — some regions have moved to sharply limit or void non-competes while others still enforce them — and you should never induce a candidate to breach confidentiality, misappropriate trade secrets, or violate a valid customer non-solicit. The clean version of this play is patient relationship-building: identify the two or three revenue leaders at adjacent (not directly competitive) companies whose growth numbers you admire, build a genuine relationship over months, and be ready when their equity vests or their company hits a ceiling. LinkedIn, industry conferences, RevOps and sales-leadership communities, and CRO peer groups are all legitimate sourcing surfaces. The trade-off is time and your own bandwidth — direct sourcing is "free" in fees but expensive in founder hours, and it lacks the confidentiality a retained firm provides when you don't want the market to know you're hiring.

There is also a quieter risk in over-relying on your own network: you tend to hire people who look like the people you already know, which narrows the funnel exactly when you most need range. Warm-channel sourcing is fast and high-trust, but it can quietly filter out strong candidates who don't happen to orbit your existing graph — which frequently means filtering out candidates from different backgrounds, sectors, or geographies than your current team. If you go the direct route, deliberately widen the top of the funnel before you narrow it: ask each investor and advisor not just "who do you know?" but "who's the best revenue leader you've seen run this exact motion, even if you don't know them well?" The other discipline direct sourcing demands is a real close process. Because there's no firm managing the timeline, founder-run searches routinely stall in the messy middle — a promising candidate goes quiet, a counteroffer materializes, or the founder gets pulled into a fundraise and lets the process drift for three weeks. Assign one person to own cadence, keep every serious candidate warm with a standing weekly touch, and treat the offer stage with the same urgency you'd bring to closing a marquee customer, because a great CRO candidate is being courted exactly like one.

## How much does it cost to hire a CRO through each channel?

Cost has two components people constantly conflate: the **search/placement fee** and the **compensation package** itself. On the search fee, retained firms customarily charge in the neighborhood of one-third of first-year cash compensation, billed in installments over the search regardless of outcome. Contingency and specialist recruiters typically charge a percentage of first-year compensation but only on a successful hire, so your risk profile is different even when the headline percentage looks similar. Fractional CROs are usually billed on a monthly retainer or day rate, which makes them the lowest-commitment option to start. Direct sourcing carries no external fee but consumes internal time and sometimes a referral bonus. I'm deliberately not quoting hard dollar figures for compensation because CRO packages swing enormously with company stage, sector, equity mix, and geography — anchoring on a single number would mislead you.

The more useful way to think about cost is total cost to a good outcome, not the invoice. A cheap contingency placement that turns over in nine months is far more expensive than a well-run retained search that lands a leader who stays four years, because CRO turnover destroys pipeline, resets the sales org, and stalls revenue during the gap. The chart below frames the trade-off across the four channels so you can weigh fee against fit-risk rather than chasing the lowest sticker.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Retained big five] --> B[High fee and high fit for senior mandates]
    C[Specialist GTM search] --> D[Moderate fee and strong startup fit]
    E[Fractional marketplace] --> F[Low commitment and fast to start]
    G[Direct network sourcing] --> H[No fee but high founder time]
    B --> I[Choose by stage budget and role clarity]
    D --> I
    F --> I
    H --> I
```

The honest conclusion is that no channel is cheapest in every dimension. Retained search minimizes fit-risk and founder time but maximizes fee. Direct sourcing minimizes fee but maximizes founder time. Fractional minimizes commitment. Match the channel to the constraint that actually binds you. For a framework on modeling the full cost of a bad revenue-leader hire, including the pipeline stall, see https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/cost-of-cro-turnover.

When you build the business case for the board, model three numbers, not one. The first is the *fee* — straightforward, and the smallest of the three. The second is the *fully loaded first-year cost of the hire* — base, variable, equity, benefits, and the ramp period during which the CRO is spending but not yet producing. The third, and the one founders most often ignore, is the *cost of getting it wrong*: the months of stalled pipeline before you admit the hire isn't working, the severance, the second search, and the trust the sales team loses each time leadership churns. When you put those three numbers side by side, the logic of paying a real fee for a well-run process usually becomes obvious, because the fee is rounding error against a mis-hire. This is also why the cheapest-looking channel is rarely the cheapest channel. Negotiate the fee if you can — retained firms will sometimes structure a portion as a flat fee, cap it, or offer a replacement guarantee if the hire leaves within the first year — but negotiate on structure and guarantees, not just on percentage, because a firm that discounts hard on price is often a firm that will under-invest in the research your search actually depends on.

## How do I evaluate whether a CRO from a given company will actually fit?

The source company on a résumé is a signal, not a verdict. A CRO who thrived at a category-leading enterprise with a mature brand and an inbound engine may flounder at a startup that needs someone to personally close the first fifty deals and build the motion from zero. The evaluation question is not "what logo are they from?" but "does the revenue motion they've mastered match the motion you need next?" A leader from a product-led-growth company is a different animal from one who built an enterprise field-sales org, and hiring the wrong archetype is a more common failure than hiring a weak individual. Build a scorecard around the specific motion, deal size, sales-cycle length, and org scale you're moving toward — then test candidates against it regardless of their pedigree.

Reference-checking is where source-company reputation becomes actionable. Backchannel references — people who worked *for* the candidate, not just the ones they hand you — tell you whether they built durable pipeline or rode a rising market. Ask former direct reports what the candidate personally built versus inherited, how they handled a bad quarter, and whether the revenue they claim was net-new motion or expansion on existing accounts. The best CRO hires often come from companies one or two stages ahead of yours, where the leader has already solved the problems you're about to face but hasn't yet outgrown the hands-on scrappiness your stage still demands. Pair that fit-analysis with a structured first-ninety-day plan so you can measure the hire against real leading indicators — pipeline coverage, ramp, and forecast accuracy — rather than waiting a full year for the revenue number to tell you. The RevOps fundamentals behind those leading indicators are covered at https://pulserevops.com/knowledge/revenue-leading-indicators.

Watch specifically for the "tailwind trap": a candidate who posted spectacular numbers at a company that was, at the time, a rocket ship in a category that was itself expanding. Great markets make average leaders look brilliant, and the résumé rarely distinguishes between a CRO who *built* the growth engine and one who happened to be standing next to it when the market lifted. Probe for what they did in the hard quarter — the year the category cooled, the competitor that ate their lunch, the pricing change that broke the model — because that is where you learn whether they can operate without a tailwind, which is exactly the condition most companies hire a CRO to survive. Equally, weigh the *scale-down* risk as heavily as the scale-up one: an executive who ran a two-hundred-person revenue org at a public company may have spent years managing managers and forecasting to Wall Street, and may genuinely not want to sit on demos and rebuild a comp plan from scratch. Neither profile is better in the abstract; the only question that matters is whether the work they'll actually do in your first year is work they still find energizing. Test that directly — walk them through the least glamorous, most hands-on task the role will demand in month two, and watch whether they lean in or visibly deflate. The candidate who lights up at the unglamorous work is usually the one who lasts.

## Related questions

### What does a Chief Revenue Officer actually do?
A CRO owns all revenue-generating functions — sales, and often marketing, customer success, and revenue operations — aligning them under one accountable leader so pipeline, conversion, and retention are managed as a single system rather than siloed teams.

### When should a startup hire its first CRO?
Usually after product-market fit is proven and repeatable revenue exists, when the founder can no longer personally run sales and the company needs a system-builder to scale the motion — often around Series B, though a fractional CRO can bridge earlier.

### Is a fractional CRO worth it?
Often yes for pre-scale companies: you get senior go-to-market judgment on pricing, comp, and pipeline without a full permanent package, and it de-risks the eventual full-time search by clarifying exactly what the role needs.

### How long does a CRO search take?
A retained or specialist search commonly runs a few months from kickoff to signed offer, longer for confidential or highly specialized mandates; direct network sourcing can be faster or far slower depending on timing and candidate availability.

### Should marketing report to the CRO?
It depends on your model — many companies unify sales, marketing, and customer success under the CRO to align the full revenue funnel, while others keep marketing separate; the right answer follows your go-to-market motion, not a rule.

## FAQ

**Which executive search firm is best for hiring a CRO?**
There is no single best firm — the right choice depends on your stage. The big five (Spencer Stuart, Heidrick & Struggles, Korn Ferry, Russell Reynolds, Egon Zehnder) excel at enterprise and PE-backed searches, while specialist growth-stage firms like True Search and Daversa Partners are often a stronger, faster fit for venture-backed startups.

**Can I hire a CRO without using a search firm?**
Yes. Many CROs are hired directly through investor networks, board introductions, and the CEO's own leadership graph. This carries no external fee but requires significant founder time and lacks the confidentiality and market-mapping a retained firm provides.

**What is the typical fee to hire a CRO through retained search?**
Retained firms customarily charge in the region of one-third of the executive's first-year cash compensation, billed in installments over the course of the search regardless of whether a placement is ultimately made.

**What is a fractional CRO and when does it make sense?**
A fractional CRO is an experienced revenue leader engaged part-time, usually on a monthly retainer, to build or fix the go-to-market engine before a company is ready for a full-time hire. It makes sense for pre-scale companies that need senior judgment without a permanent package.

**Is it legal to hire a CRO away from a competitor?**
Generally yes, but you must respect valid agreements — non-compete enforceability varies widely by jurisdiction, and you must never induce a candidate to breach confidentiality, misappropriate trade secrets, or violate a valid customer non-solicitation clause. When in doubt, get legal counsel.

**How do I know if a CRO from a big-name company will fit my startup?**
Match the revenue motion, not the logo. A leader who scaled an enterprise field-sales org may struggle at a startup that needs hands-on founder-style selling. Build a scorecard around your specific deal size, sales cycle, and org stage, and backchannel-reference the candidate against it.

**Should I use a contingency recruiter or a retained firm for a CRO?**
Retained search suits true C-suite mandates where confidentiality and off-market sourcing matter and you want committed research. Contingency and specialist recruiters work well for revenue-leader roles just below the C-suite or when you want to pay only on a successful placement.

**How long will a newly hired CRO take to show results?**
Expect a ramp measured in quarters, not weeks. Judge the hire early on leading indicators — pipeline coverage, forecast accuracy, and rep ramp — rather than waiting a full year for the top-line revenue number to confirm the fit.

**Can my investors help me find a CRO?**
Very often yes, and it is usually the first place to look if you're funded. Venture and PE firms keep talent partners and operating-partner networks specifically to connect portfolio companies with vetted revenue leaders, frequently at no fee and with better context than an outside firm because they already know your business.

**What should I look for in a CRO's references?**
Prioritize backchannel references — former direct reports and peers, not just the names the candidate offers. Ask what the candidate personally built versus inherited, how they handled a down quarter, and whether their claimed revenue was net-new motion or expansion on an already-growing base.

**Do I need a full-time CRO, or is a VP of Sales enough?**
If you need one motion executed well and the founder still sets strategy, a strong VP of Sales may be the better and cheaper hire. A CRO makes sense when you need one accountable leader unifying sales, marketing, customer success, and RevOps into a single revenue system.

**How do I avoid over-paying for a CRO search?**
Match the channel to your stage rather than defaulting to a big-five retainer, negotiate on structure and replacement guarantees rather than headline percentage, and model the fully loaded cost of a mis-hire so you weigh fee against fit-risk instead of chasing the lowest sticker price.
